questions.question: Critics of one kernel design blame its performance penalty on the extra message passing needed every time an application talks to a file-system or driver server, while praising how a crashed server can simply be restarted. Which design is this?
questions.explanation: Microkernels run services in user space, so every client-server interaction is an IPC hop — the classic performance cost — while gaining the fault isolation that lets dead servers be restarted.

questions.question: In Linux, the VFS, scheduler, and all drivers share one privileged address space, so a syscall stays in-process and fast — but a single buggy driver can panic the whole machine. Which kernel organization is this?
questions.explanation: A monolithic kernel runs every service in kernel space: calls between layers are ordinary function calls (fast), yet any kernel-space fault can bring down the entire system.

questions.question: A profiler shows a benchmark spending 40% of its time trapping into the kernel just to call gettimeofday(). Linux kills that overhead by mapping a small kernel-provided page into each process so the call runs entirely in user space. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: The vDSO maps kernel-exported functions like gettimeofday() into the process image, so read-only, frequently used calls execute without a mode switch or context-switch cost.

questions.question: To squeeze more performance out of a VM, its guest kernel is recompiled so every privileged operation calls straight into the hypervisor instead of executing a trapping instruction. Which virtualization approach is this?
questions.explanation: Paravirtualization modifies the guest to issue explicit hypercalls, eliminating trap-and-emulate overhead for privileged work — at the price of needing a modified guest OS.

questions.question: On x86, kernel code runs in ring 0 and browsers in ring 3; hardware refuses a ring-3 attempt to touch a ring-0 structure. What is this hardware-enforced privilege hierarchy called?
questions.explanation: Protection rings give hardware-graded privilege levels from ring 0 (most trusted) to ring 3 (least), so user code cannot directly execute or touch kernel-only resources.

questions.question: Before an x86 CPU permits an I/O instruction, it checks the two least-significant bits of the CS register. What is the name of the privilege value stored in those bits?
questions.explanation: The Current Privilege Level lives in the low two bits of CS: 0 while running kernel code and 3 in user code, and the hardware gates privileged instructions and memory access on it.

questions.question: A user program issues int 0x80; the CPU reads the corresponding IDT entry, finds a gate whose DPL allows a ring-3 caller, and makes a controlled jump into kernel code. What kind of gate descriptor permitted the switch?
questions.explanation: A trap gate (or call/system gate) descriptor names the handler and the privilege a caller needs; it is the controlled doorway that lets ring-3 code enter the kernel safely.

questions.question: An interrupt handler must guard a two-instruction update to a kernel list on an SMP machine, and it cannot sleep in this context. Which mutual-exclusion primitive busy-waits instead of blocking?
questions.explanation: Spinlocks loop atomically until the lock frees. They are correct in interrupt context — where sleeping is impossible — and cheap for very short critical sections.

questions.question: A high-priority task becomes ready while a low-priority task is mid-syscall, but must wait for that call to finish because this kernel refuses to interrupt kernel execution. Which kernel model is this?
questions.explanation: A non-preemptive kernel runs each system call to completion before rescheduling, which simplifies kernel data structures but adds latency for high-priority or real-time work.

questions.question: To hit sub-millisecond response for a real-time task, a kernel is rebuilt so a higher-priority thread may preempt even code running inside a syscall at defined preemption points. Which kernel model is this?
questions.explanation: A preemptive kernel can switch away from a task mid-syscall, bounding worst-case latency — at the cost of needing rigorous synchronization throughout kernel code.

questions.question: On x86-64, glibc ends a getpid() stub with a single instruction that jumps straight to the address held in the LSTAR MSR, skipping the full interrupt-gate machinery. Which instruction is it?
questions.explanation: syscall loads RIP from LSTAR, saves the return address in RCX, and switches to kernel mode in a few cycles — far cheaper than a trap through the IDT.

questions.question: A kernel boots but its storage driver lives as a module on the root filesystem it cannot yet mount. Boot breaks the cycle by unpacking a small compressed image into RAM as a temporary root first. What is that image?
questions.explanation: The initramfs is an early root filesystem loaded into RAM holding the drivers and scripts needed to find and mount the real root device before pivoting to it.

questions.question: A NIC interrupt fires; the top half acks the device and schedules deferred work that runs later in interrupt context, is statically defined in the kernel, and unlike tasklets cannot be created dynamically. Which bottom-half mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Softirqs are the compile-time-fixed bottom-half mechanism running in interrupt context; tasklets are built on them but dynamically created, and workqueues run in process context.

questions.question: A ps listing shows PID 0 accumulating CPU only when every real task sleeps, and it was never created by fork() from user space — it exists from before init. Which kernel task is this?
questions.explanation: The swapper, or per-CPU idle task, is the hand-created PID 0 that spins when nothing is runnable; it is also the ancestor of init and kthreadd.

questions.question: A driver writer puts mutex_lock() inside a hard IRQ handler and the machine deadlocks, because this execution context has no process to put to sleep and reschedule. Which context rule was violated?
questions.explanation: Interrupt (atomic) context has no task_struct to block, so sleeping is impossible: a mutex or any might-sleep call inside a hard IRQ handler can hang the kernel.

questions.question: A running process invokes the read() system call. List the CPU mode transitions that occur.
questions.answer: User mode to kernel mode to user mode
alternatives: User mode, kernel mode, then back to user mode
questions.explanation: The system-call instruction traps into kernel mode; after the kernel performs the I/O, it returns and restores user mode.

questions.question: A user-space program executes a privileged instruction such as disabling interrupts. What does the CPU do?
questions.explanation: Hardware checks the mode bit; a privileged opcode in user mode triggers a protection exception that transfers control to the OS.

questions.question: A file-system module crashes. On which kernel design would that failure be confined to a user-space server instead of panicking the whole OS?
questions.explanation: Microkernels run file systems as user-space servers, so a crash there can be restarted without corrupting the kernel.

questions.question: The IDTR register holds the IDT base address 0x8001000, each gate descriptor is 16 bytes, and interrupt vector 0x21 arrives. At which memory address does the CPU fetch the handler's descriptor?
questions.explanation: The CPU indexes the IDT with the vector number: base + vector x 16 = 0x8001000 + 0x21 x 16 = 0x8001000 + 0x210 = 0x8001210.

questions.question: A system call must receive a large buffer that cannot fit in CPU registers. Which parameter-passing method is used?
questions.answer: Pass a pointer to a memory block
alternatives: Parameters in a block/table in memory with the address in a register
questions.explanation: For large data, parameters are stored in a memory block or table and only its address is passed in a register.
